transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Hello, Mrs. Al-Rashid. I wanted to come in and speak with you personally about what happened during your infusion earlier today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Hello, doctor.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know the nurse mentioned some things to you already, but I want to be very clear about this. We made a mistake. Your anti-nausea medication was not included in the chemotherapy order, and that is why you experienced such severe vomiting.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I... I see. I was told there was a problem.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry that this happened. It was our responsibility to ensure those medications were ordered, and we failed to do that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It was very frightening. I thought perhaps the chemotherapy was too strong for me, or that I was reacting badly to the medicine itself.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That sounds like a terrifying experience, especially when you aren't sure why your body is reacting that way.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I have always trusted the doctors here. I did not expect this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: This is a very difficult conversation to have, and I know it may feel unsettling to hear a doctor admit to a mistake. Please take all the time you need.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just... I don't understand how it can be forgotten. These medicines are so important.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is hard to wrap my head around it too, but the order for the pre-meds simply wasn't entered into the system. It was a failure in our process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And now I feel so weak.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see how exhausted you are after going through that. It's completely understandable that you feel drained after such a violent reaction.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Will it happen again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are going to make sure it does not. First, I have already manually entered the anti-emetics into your chart for every single upcoming session. I have also flagged your file with a high-priority alert that requires the nurse to double-verify the pre-meds before the infusion starts.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I do not want to be a burden to the nurses.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are not a burden. This is our job. I've also scheduled a follow-up call with you tomorrow morning at ten to see how your stomach is settling and to make sure you are hydrating.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Tomorrow morning.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, I will call you personally. In the meantime, I want you to tell the nurse immediately if you feel any more nausea tonight, even if it's mild. We have a different medication we can give you right now if you're still feeling sick.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I think I am just tired now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That makes sense. It has been a very long and stressful day.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are very kind to tell me this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I want to be honest with you. You deserve to know exactly what is happening with your care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just hope the next time is better.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am committed to making sure it is. To make sure we are on the same page, do you feel comfortable with the plan for the next visit and the call tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, I think I understand.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll be thinking of you tonight. I'll call you at ten tomorrow. Please try to rest.

H.justification: Resident allows full pauses, never interrupts, and uses a patient, regulated pace throughout the conversation.

E.justification: Error named explicitly in the first turn, lay language used, and comprehension checked at the end ('do you feel comfortable with the plan...').

A.justification: Direct apology used ('I am sorry'), responsibility explicitly taken ('our responsibility... we failed'), and no deflection.

R.justification: Specific emotions named back ('terrifying experience', 'exhausted', 'stressful day') and engages with the patient's emotional bids.

T.justification: Includes specific next steps with timelines (call tomorrow at 10), patient role (tell nurse immediately if nausea occurs), and prevention (manual entry and high-priority alert).
